notes: Clean provision-time collection with a dynamic flag, and the strongest end-to-end tests, covering both request-only expressions and every response placeholder type, including dynamic names that still trigger retries.

Clean provision-time collection using MatchDescendants/FunctionMatcher, with exact-name plus header-prefix classification and conservative dynamic handling; strong tests show request-only expressions pass through and each response placeholder, including the dynamic name case, still triggers retries.

Precomputes placeholder names correctly with good unit and integration tests, but isResponsePlaceholder lowercases names without need, which contradicts its own comment that names are compared exactly (harmless but sloppy).

Correctly records literal and dynamic ph() names at provision time and classifies response placeholders by exact name or header prefix, with thorough unit and integration tests; the unexplained strings.ToLower in isResponsePlaceholder is a questionable extra that makes differently-cased names count as response placeholders.

The logic is correct, but it keeps the checked AST and walks it on every proxied response inside PlaceholderNames, which adds needless per-request work and allocation on a hot path; its integration tests cover all the maintainer-specified request-only cases and the ph() response retry.

Classification logic is correct, but it keeps the checked AST and re-walks it on every PlaceholderNames() call, which runs on every proxied response in the hot path; tests cover request-only cases and the ph() response case well but do not unit-test the full response-placeholder list.

Collects literal ph() names at provision time and flags non-literal names as dynamic, then checks them against exact response placeholder names plus the header prefix; it matches the reference and has thorough unit and integration tests, including a check that the POST body is preserved.

Mirrors the reference approach closely, collecting placeholder names and the dynamic flag at provision time and doing exact or prefix classification; good unit tests for both Placeholders() and matcherSetReadsResponse, plus an integration test checking that the upstream receives the body once.

A neat ReferencesPlaceholder(predicate) API over precomputed names keeps the reverseproxy check to one line; it has a broad matcher-set table and an integration test that echoes the body, though there is no direct celmatcher unit test.

Elegant ReferencesPlaceholder(predicate) API computed at provision time, folding the dynamic case into the check; a comprehensive classification table (comprehensions, is_transport_error, near-miss names, escaped literals) plus an integration test that verifies the body passes through.

Close to the reference and correct (hidden tests pass), but the zip Open path has an odd symlink-only seek-past-end hack, a symlink and a regular .rclonelink of the same name produce duplicate listings, and the squashfs test depends on mksquashfs being installed.

The zip side is close to the reference and squashfs works via a double lookup in NewObject, but the root/expectedRemote logic is convoluted and the symlink-only offset special case in zip Open is a hack.

Symlink handling mostly works, but the large readZip rewrite regresses one case: a regular root like 'real.rclonelink' is exposed as 'real' even without --links; it also silently drops members below links and slips in an unrelated CheckClose fix.

Functional, with regular-file priority and root handling, but hides archive members below a symlink rather than exposing them; it also heavily rewrites readZip into two passes and includes an unrelated CheckClose tweak.

Solid on both backends: List and NewObject agree, regular .rclonelink members win over links, and a root naming a symlink without the suffix gets an errLinksNeedsSuffix-style error matching the local backend; tests are good but there is no copy or hostile-archive test.

A clean implementation that mirrors the local backend (ErrLinksNeedsSuffix for unsuffixed symlink roots) and resolves regular-vs-symlink clashes consistently in both List and NewObject; its tests are solid but lack copy and escape coverage.

The zip side is reasonable, but squashfs NewObject strips or rejects any '.rclonelink' name, so regular members ending in .rclonelink are listed yet unreachable via NewObject in both modes; the zip root suffix trim also misbehaves for directories named '*.rclonelink', and there are no squashfs tests.

Zip is fine, but squashfs NewObject strips or rejects any .rclonelink name, so a regular member ending in .rclonelink can never be looked up and List and NewObject disagree; there are no squashfs tests.

Clean and correct with strong tests including copy and hostile-archive checks, but it has no clash handling (duplicate listing) and it changed squashfs f.file to drop prefixSlash, which breaks single-file roots when a prefix is set.

Implements both backends as the spec asks and handles symlink roots with or without the suffix; squashfs lookup lets a regular .rclonelink file win, and the tests are thorough (copy, skip, escape, ranges, squashfs testdata); one small risk is that squashfs f.file drops prefixSlash.

Thoughtful design: a shared case-insensitive LinkFilter, an OpenLink helper, and a dirEntries function guarantee List and NewObject agree, but it is a large refactor and it can hide regular .rclonelink members or drop links rather than expose them as the reference does.

Over-engineered shared LinkFilter that drops symlinks, and even regular .rclonelink files, on case-insensitive clashes, contrary to the spec; squashfs newObjectNative now rebuilds every entry in the directory on each lookup.

Meets the spec, and is more defensive than the reference: it reads zip link targets and drops any link that clashes with a regular entry, a directory or a member beneath it, which keeps hostile copies safe, but addLinks pokes at dirtree internals (`(*dt)[dir] = nil`) and the drop-instead-of-list behaviour likely caused the hidden test failure.
Works and handles clashes, but instead of exposing a symlink it silently drops any symlink that has members beneath it (a deviation from the spec), and addLinks pokes directly into dirtree internals.

A well-documented refcounted unixSocket with release under unixSocketsMu, an ownership-guarded unlink and Linux/Android-only abstract detection matching the reference; it also guards deleteListener, but the restructured internals break the hidden white-box tests.

Correct refcounted design with an ownership-checked unlink and Linux/Android-only abstract detection, plus thorough tests, but it restructures listenReusable and changes the deleteListener semantics more than needed, and its internal API diverges, so the hidden tests fail.

Close takes the lock, uses a CAS guard that returns net.ErrClosed, reference-counts a master fd and only unlinks when the socket still owns the map key, which fixes the leak and the race in substance; it fails all hidden tests, most likely because the reshaped unixSockets map and wrapper fields no longer match the white-box internals the tests use.

A tidy closeUnixSocket helper keeps the lock, CAS and ownership-checked unlink in one place, and the fix is focused; abstract detection is not OS-restricted, and the removed count field breaks the hidden tests.

The fix logic is solid (lock-held release, ownership check, unlinkUnixSocket helper, deleteListener guard), but the patch leaves a stray debugging file `.cwd-probe` at the repo root and still fails all hidden tests.

Behaviorally similar to the others, with a master fd, lock-guarded release and an ownership check, but it leaves a stray '.cwd-probe' debugging file and an unrelated listeners.go comment, treats '@' as abstract on all OSes, and fails the hidden tests.

Cleanly fixes the leaked dup fd and the unlink path using a shared unixSocket with a mutex-guarded refcount, a CAS close guard and abstract-name skipping; it leaves deleteListener alone and its tests are thorough, but the internal restructure is incompatible with the hidden tests.

A clean, focused redesign: a shared unixSocket holds the master fd, releases under the lock with an ownership check, and returns net.ErrClosed exactly; however, '@' is treated as abstract on every OS, and the changed struct shape breaks the hidden tests.

Appears functionally sound but over-engineers the fix: it adds a second mutex, changes listenerPool registration for reused sockets, rewrites listenReusable flow and edits the listeners.go chmod error path, all well beyond the needed change.

Adds a second mutex, wraps reused sockets in deleteListener (changing listenerPool usage counts) and edits listeners.go to close on chmod failure; the logic seems sound but has more moving parts and scope than needed, abstract detection is an inline OS-agnostic check, and the hidden tests fail.

The master-fd refcount design works and guards deleteListener against double close; however, a second close returns the wrapped OpError rather than net.ErrClosed, release unlinks without checking map ownership, and it fails the hidden tests.

A refcounted shared master fd fixes the leaked File() dups, checks abstract sockets per OS and guards double close, but the second Close returns the wrapped underlying error rather than net.ErrClosed, release unlinks without checking map ownership, and the struct redesign diverges from what the hidden tests expect, so they fail.
